notes.21:1: Vulgate chapter 21 begins five verses earlier than the Hebrew Masoretic Text and most modern English Bibles (Vulgate 21:1-5 corresponds to MT 20:45-49, and Vulgate 21:6-37 to MT 21:1-32).
notes.21:2: Latin "stilla" literally means "drip" or "drop," a prophetic idiom for uttering words (repeated in 21:7). The Vulgate also distinguishes three southerly terms: "auster" (south), "africus" (southwest), and "meridianus" (southern).
notes.21:15: Vulgate-distinct reading: Latin "qui moves sceptrum filii mei, succidisti omne lignum" ("you who move the scepter of My son, you have cut down every tree") renders an obscure Hebrew line differently from the Masoretic Text ("Shall we rejoice? The rod of my son despises every tree"). Similarly, 21:17-18 follows the Vulgate's distinct clauses ("who had fled" and "when it overthrows the scepter").
notes.21:24: Vulgate-distinct reading: Latin "manu capiet conjecturam ... conjiciet" ("with his hand he will take a conjecture ... he will conjecture") depicts the king divining at the crossroads, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text instructs the prophet to carve a signpost.
notes.21:28: Vulgate-distinct reading: Latin "sabbatorum otium imitans" ("imitating the rest of the Sabbaths") connects the Hebrew phrase for sworn oaths with the Sabbath. In 21:32, the Vulgate likewise renders the Hebrew term for "ruin" as "iniquitatem" ("iniquity").
notes.22:16: Vulgate-distinct reading: Latin "possidebo te" ("I will possess you") reflects a first-person verb of possessing or inheriting, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "you will be profaned in yourself."
notes.22:20: Vulgate-distinct reading: Latin "requiescam" ("I will rest") interprets the Hebrew verb as "rest" rather than "leave/deposit," and in 22:21 "succendam vos" reads "I will kindle you" where the Masoretic Text has "I will blow upon you."
notes.22:28: Latin "liniebant eos absque temperamento" literally describes plastering or daubing without proper tempering (an allusion to flimsy whitewash or untempered mortar, as in Ezekiel 13:10-15).
notes.22:30: Vulgate-distinct reading: Latin "qui interponeret sepem, et staret oppositus contra me" ("who would put up a hedge and stand in opposition against Me") corresponds to the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "build up the wall and stand in the breach before Me."
notes.23:10: The Vulgate reads plural "and the women became notorious" (factae sunt famosae mulieres), whereas the Hebrew text reads singular ("she became a byword among women").
notes.23:17: The Vulgate translates "to the bed of breasts" (ad cubile mammarum), reading the Hebrew consonantal term for "love" as "breasts," and renders "her soul was satiated by them" (saturata est) where the Hebrew means "alienated" (similarly in vv. 22 and 28).
notes.23:23: The Vulgate translates three titles as common nouns ("nobles, and tyrants, and princes") where the Hebrew text lists proper names of Mesopotamian tribes or regions (Pekod, Shoa, and Koa).
notes.23:32: In Latin, the feminine relative clause "which is most capacious" (quae est capacissima) attaches grammatically to feminine "derision" (subsannationem) because Latin "cup" (calix) is masculine, whereas in the Hebrew it refers to the large capacity of the feminine "cup."
notes.23:42: The Vulgate renders "came from the desert" (veniebant de deserto) where the Hebrew contains a disputed term often translated "drunkards" or "Sabeans," and uses the masculine pronoun (eorum) for "their hands" and "their heads."
notes.24:5: Latin strues ossium ("piles of bones", echoed by ossa in v. 10) translates the Hebrew consonants literally as bones used for fuel, whereas many modern versions emend the Hebrew to "wood" or "logs." The Vulgate also renders the second half of the verse with perfect indicatives ("has boiled up... have been boiled thoroughly") rather than imperatives.
notes.24:7: Latin limpidissimam petram (lit. "most clear/gleaming rock", recurring in 24:8 and 26:4, 14) renders Hebrew tzechich sela ("bare, sun-bleached rock"), emphasizing a smooth surface completely stripped of dust.
notes.24:17: Latin corona ("crown", also in v. 23) translates Hebrew pe'er ("turban/headdress"), and cibos lugentium ("the food of mourners", also in v. 22) explicitly interprets Hebrew "bread of men."
notes.24:21: Vulgate super quo pavet anima vestra ("that over which your soul is in dread") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "the compassion/longing of your soul"; contrast v. 25, where the Vulgate has requiescunt ("rest").
notes.24:27: Vulgate et scietis is second-person plural ("and you [pl.] will know"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads third-person plural ("and they will know").
notes.25:4: Latin caulas suas ("their sheepfolds") renders Hebrew tirotehem ("their encampments"), reflecting a pastoral reading of the eastern invaders' settlements.
notes.25:6: Vulgate ex toto affectu ("with all your passion/feeling") renders a rare Hebrew phrase meaning "with all scorn of soul" in a more general emotional sense (compare toto animo in v. 15).
notes.25:13: Vulgate ab austro ("from the south") translates the Hebrew place name Teman according to its literal geographical meaning.
notes.25:14: In vv. 12-14a the Vulgate uses the Greco-Latin regional name Idumaea ("Idumea") for Edom before switching directly to Edom in the second half of v. 14.
notes.25:16: Vulgate interficiam interfectores ("I will kill the killers") translates the Hebrew gentilic Keretim ("Cherethites") etymologically as a cognate noun of destruction; in vv. 15-16 Latin Palaestini is Jerome's standard rendering for the Philistines.
notes.26:9: Latin vineas et arietes ("siege sheds and battering rams") adapts Roman military terminology—vineae being movable protective shelters—to render Hebrew "the blow of his battering ram," while in armatura sua ("with his weaponry") renders Hebrew "with his axes/swords."
notes.26:16: Vulgate super repentino casu tuo ("at your sudden fall") takes the Hebrew phrase usually rendered "every moment" (lirga'im) in the sense of suddenness.
notes.26:18: Vulgate naves ("ships") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "coastlands/islands" (ha-iyim), and eo quod nullus egrediatur ex te ("because no one goes out from you") interprets Hebrew mi-tzetekh ("at your departure").
notes.26:20: Vulgate populum sempiternum ("the everlasting people") renders Hebrew am olam ("people of old"), and porro cum dedero gloriam ("moreover, when I give glory") construes the clause temporally as leading into v. 21's main verb, in nihilum redigam te ("I will reduce you to nothing," where Hebrew reads "a terror").
notes.27:6: Vulgate "from Indian ivory, and little cabins from the islands of Italy" (ex ebore indico, et prætoriola de insulis Italiæ) is a distinctly Latin rendering where the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to boxwood or cypress decks from the coastlands of Kittim (Cyprus).
notes.27:11: Vulgate "Pygmies" (Pigmæi) translates Hebrew Gammadim by linking it to a root meaning "cubit," and "quivers" (pharetras) corresponds to Hebrew "shields."
notes.27:12: Vulgate identifies Hebrew Tarshish as "the Carthaginians" (Carthaginenses), just as in 27:10 it renders Lud and Put as "Lydians" and "Libyans."
notes.27:16: Vulgate retains "chodchod" directly from the obscure Hebrew term kadkod, commonly understood as a precious gem such as agate or ruby.
notes.27:19: Vulgate "Mosel" treats the Hebrew preposition and place name me-Uzal ("from Uzal") as a single proper name; similarly, 27:26 has "south wind" (ventus auster) for Hebrew "east wind," and 27:28 reads "fleets" (classes) for Hebrew "coastlands/pasturelands."
notes.28:8: Vulgate "They will kill and drag you down" (Interficient, et detrahent te) renders Hebrew shahat ("the pit") verbally as "they will kill."
notes.28:12: Vulgate "seal of likeness" (signaculum similitudinis) differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("sealer of perfection/proportion"), reflecting a reading connected to "likeness" or "pattern."
notes.28:13: Vulgate renders Hebrew "Eden, the garden of God" as "the delights of the paradise of God" (in deliciis paradisi Dei). "Openings" translates Latin foramina (literally "holes/perforations/sockets"), reflecting the root of Hebrew neqabeka (often taken as pipes or gem settings).
notes.28:14: Vulgate "outstretched" (extentus) derives Hebrew mimshah ("anointed") from a root meaning "to stretch out" or "measure."
notes.28:18: Vulgate has singular "your sanctification" (sanctificationem tuam, the Vulgate's standard rendering of Hebrew miqdash, "sanctuary"), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has plural "your sanctuaries."
notes.29:1: Vulgate reads "eleventh day" (undecima die), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "twelfth day."
notes.29:3: Vulgate reads "and I made myself" (et ego feci memetipsum), emphasizing Pharaoh's boast of self-creation (contrast v. 9, et ego feci eum, "and I made it"), whereas the Hebrew can be read "I made it for myself."
notes.29:10: Vulgate renders Hebrew mi-migdol seveneh ("from Migdol to Syene") as "from the tower of Syene" (a turre Syenes), taking migdol as the common noun "tower," and uses the classical name "Ethiopia" (Aethiopiae) for Hebrew Cush.
notes.29:16: Vulgate reads "teaching iniquity so that they flee and follow them" (docentes iniquitatem ut fugiant, et sequantur eos), whereas the Hebrew reads "bringing iniquity to remembrance when they turn after them."
notes.29:19: Latin literally reads dabo Nabuchodonosor regem Babylonis in terra Aegypti ("I will give/place Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon in the land of Egypt"), making Nebuchadnezzar the direct object rather than the indirect object as in v. 20 (dedi ei terram Aegypti). In v. 18, the Vulgate also adds mihi ("served Me").
notes.30:5: Vulgate uses Greco-Roman names ("Ethiopia" for Hebrew Cush, "Libya" for Put, "the Lydians" for Lud) and renders Hebrew kol ha'erev ("all the mixed people") as "all the rest of the common people" (omne reliquum vulgus).
notes.30:9: Vulgate specifies "in triremes" (in trieribus) where the Hebrew simply reads "in ships," and "without a doubt" (absque dubio) where the Hebrew reads "behold."
notes.30:14: Across vv. 13-17, the Vulgate substitutes Greco-Roman city names for the Hebrew names: Memphis (for Noph), Alexandria (for No/Thebes), Pelusium (for Sin), Heliopolis (for Aven/On), and Bubastis (for Pi-beseth). In v. 17, ipsae captivae is feminine plural, referring to the cities themselves (or their female inhabitants).
notes.30:16: Vulgate reads "daily distresses" (angustiae quotidianae), whereas the Hebrew reads "adversaries by day."
notes.30:22: Vulgate reads singular "his arm, strong yet broken" (brachium ejus forte, sed confractum), whereas the Hebrew reads plural "his arms, both the strong one and the broken one." In v. 24, the Clementine Vulgate also reads plural gement ("they will groan") where the Hebrew has singular "he will groan."
notes.31:6: Vulgate opens v. 6 with "And when it had stretched out its shadow" (Cumque extendisset umbram suam), translating a phrase placed at the end of v. 5 in the Hebrew ("when it sent them out").
notes.31:9: Here and in vv. 16 and 18, the Vulgate translates Hebrew Eden etymologically as "delight" (ligna voluptatis, "trees of delight"), and renders Hebrew gan ("garden") as "paradise" (paradisus, vv. 8-9).
notes.31:15: Vulgate reads "I covered it with the deep" (operui eum abysso), whereas the Hebrew reads "I covered the deep over it"; here and in vv. 16-17, inferos/infernum ("the underworld") renders Hebrew Sheol.
notes.31:17: Vulgate reads future "will go down" (descendent) and "and the arm of each one will sit under its shade" (et brachium uniuscujusque sedebit sub umbraculo ejus), differing in tense and wording from the Hebrew ("they went down... its allies who lived under its shadow").
notes.31:18: Vulgate uses the perfect passive "you have been led down" (deductus es) and "you will sleep" (dormies), where the Hebrew has "you will be brought down" and "you will lie."
notes.32:2: Vulgate 'ventilabas cornu' ('thrust with a horn') reflects Jerome reading the Hebrew verb for bursting forth as goring or pushing with a horn (cf. Dan 8:4); 'draconi' renders the Hebrew sea creature as 'dragon.'
notes.32:6: Vulgate 'foetore sanguinis tui' ('the stench of your blood') diverges from the Masoretic Text ('your outflow/discharge'), just as v. 5 has 'colles tuos sanie tua' ('your hills with your gore') where the Hebrew speaks of valleys and height or carcass.
notes.32:8: The final clause ('when your wounded have fallen in the midst of the land, declares the Lord God') is distinctive to the Clementine Vulgate and absent from the Masoretic Text; 'moerere' ('mourn') also translates a Hebrew verb meaning both 'darken' and 'mourn.'
notes.32:18: The Clementine Vulgate omits verse 19 (found in the Masoretic Text and modern editions), moving directly from verse 18 to verse 20.
notes.32:30: Vulgate 'universi venatores' ('all the hunters') translates the Hebrew gentilic for 'Sidonians' etymologically from the root meaning 'to hunt.'
notes.33:2: Vulgate 'de novissimis suis' ('from the outermost among them') literally renders the Hebrew idiom for 'from their extremities/whole number,' and in Latin can also carry the sense 'from the lowest among them.'
notes.33:14: Vulgate 'egerit poenitentiam' (lit. 'does penance / repents') renders a Hebrew verb meaning simply 'turns back'; similarly in v. 16, 'non imputabuntur' ('will not be imputed') corresponds to 'will not be remembered' in the Masoretic Text.
notes.33:25: The Clementine Vulgate omits verse 26 (found in the Masoretic Text and modern editions), moving directly from verse 25 to verse 27.
notes.33:31: Vulgate 'in canticum oris sui vertunt illos' ('they turn them into a song of their mouth') diverges from the Masoretic Text, which speaks of expressing lustful or affectionate desires with their mouths; likewise v. 32 renders the Hebrew 'love song' as 'carmen musicum' ('a musical song').
notes.34:3: Latin Lac ("milk") follows the Septuagint in reading the Hebrew consonants as halab ("milk"), whereas the Masoretic Text vocalizes them as heleb ("fat").
notes.34:6: Latin non erat, inquam, qui requireret ("there was no one, I say, who searched") repeats the same verb with an emphatic parenthetical "I say," whereas the Masoretic Text uses two different verbs without "I say."
notes.34:16: Latin custodiam ("I will guard") agrees with the Septuagint against the Masoretic Text's "I will destroy," reflecting a consonant variant in the underlying Hebrew.
notes.34:25: Latin qui habitant in deserto, securi dormient in saltibus makes "those who dwell in the wilderness" the subject of "will sleep securely in the woodlands," whereas the Masoretic Text coordinates two future verbs ("they will dwell securely in the wilderness and sleep in the woods").
notes.34:29: Latin germen nominatum ("a renowned shoot") renders the Hebrew "planting of renown" with germen ("shoot/sprout"), echoing the messianic title used in the Vulgate of Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15.
notes.35:6: Latin cum sanguinem oderis ("since you hate blood," or concessively "although you hate blood") lacks the negation found in the Masoretic Text ("since you did not hate bloodshed").
notes.35:11: Latin notus efficiar per eos ("I will be made known through them") uses per ("through") where the Masoretic Text reads "among them."
notes.35:13: Latin derogastis adversum me verba vestra ("you have spoken your disparaging words against Me") interprets the verb as disparagement rather than the Masoretic Text's "multiplied your words against Me."
notes.35:15: Latin Idumæa ("Idumea") is the Greco-Latin name used by the Vulgate for Hebrew Edom.
notes.36:5: Latin Idumæa ("Idumea") represents the territory of Edom. The Vulgate's "from the soul, and cast it out to lay it waste" (et ex animo, et ejecerunt eam ut vastarent) differs from the Masoretic Hebrew, which speaks of acting with utter scorn so that the land's pasture might be for plunder.
notes.36:13: Latin suffocans ("choking"), followed by necabis ("kill") in v. 14 and amittes ("lose") in v. 15, reflects Vulgate-distinct renderings where the Masoretic Hebrew uses verbs for bereaving (v. 13) and causing to stumble (vv. 14-15).
notes.36:23: The Vulgate reads ait Dominus exercituum ("says the Lord of hosts"), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "declares the Lord God."
notes.36:25: Latin effundam ("I will pour out") echoes v. 18 (effudi, "I poured out") rather than the Hebrew verb for sprinkling.
notes.36:35: Latin hortus voluptatis ("a garden of delight") translates Hebrew "garden of Eden" by meaning, consistent with the Vulgate's rendering of Eden in Genesis.
notes.37:1: Latin campi ("plain") renders Hebrew biq'ah (a broad valley or plain) as an open plain (also in v. 2).
notes.37:5: Latin spiritus conveys both "breath" and "spirit" throughout vv. 5-10, directly linking the animating breath of the bones with spiritum meum ("My Spirit") in v. 14, while Latin ventis ("winds") is used separately in v. 9.
notes.37:16: Latin lignum ("piece of wood" or "wood") is used throughout vv. 16-20 for Hebrew etz ("wood" or "stick"). The Vulgate inscriptions shift from genitive ("Of Judah, and of the sons of Israel") on the first wood to dative ("For Joseph, the wood of Ephraim, and for all the house of Israel") on the second.
notes.37:19: The Vulgate reads in manu ejus ("in his hand," referring to Judah or the prophet), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "in My hand."
notes.37:26: Latin sanctificationem meam ("My sanctification," repeated in v. 28) translates Hebrew miqdash ("sanctuary") and pairs directly with sanctificator Israël ("the Sanctifier of Israel") in v. 28.
notes.38:2: Latin 'principem capitis' literally reads "prince of the head," rendering Hebrew 'rosh' as a common noun ("chief") rather than the proper name "Rosh" found in the Septuagint; 'terram Magog' ("the land of Magog") stands in direct apposition to Gog.
notes.38:4: Vulgate 'frenum' ("a bridle") and 'hastam' ("spear") differ from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which has "hooks" and "buckler" (large shield); similarly in 38:5 the Vulgate uses the ethnonyms 'Persae, Aethiopes, et Libyes' ("Persians, Ethiopians, and Libyans") for Hebrew "Persia, Cush, and Put."
notes.38:7: Vulgate 'esto eis in praeceptum' literally reads "be to them for a command," rendering Hebrew 'lemishmar' ("for a guard/watch") in the sense of giving orders.
notes.38:16: Vulgate 'eris' ("you will be") takes the ambiguous Hebrew form 'tihyeh' as second-person singular addressed to Gog rather than third-person feminine ("it will come to pass").
notes.38:17: Unlike the Hebrew text, which frames this as a question ("Are you the one...?"), the Vulgate reads a declarative statement ('Tu ergo ille es', "You, then, are the one...") without an interrogative particle.
notes.39:4: Following the Clementine punctuation ('feris, avibus'), 'feris' is translated as a distinct noun ("wild animals") rather than an adjective modifying 'avibus' ("birds of prey," Hebrew 'eit tzippor').
notes.39:7: Vulgate 'non polluam' is first-person active ("I will not profane"), whereas the Hebrew is commonly rendered permissively ("I will not let My holy name be profaned").
notes.39:11: Vulgate 'locum nominatum' ("a renowned place") reflects reading Hebrew 'sham' ("there") as 'shem' ("name/renown"), and 'obstupescere faciet praetereuntes' ("will cause those passing by to be astonished") diverges from the Hebrew "will block the travelers."
notes.39:18: Vulgate 'altilium, et pinguium omnium' ("fattened animals, and all fat ones") omits the place name "Bashan" found in the Hebrew ("fatlings of Bashan"), translating it instead as an adjective of fatness.
notes.39:20: Vulgate 'de equo, et equite forti' ("with horse and mighty horseman") attaches 'forti' ("mighty") directly to 'equite' ("horseman"), whereas the Hebrew lists "horses and charioteers, mighty men" separately.
notes.40:5: Latin "sex cubitorum et palmo" literally gives a total length of six cubits and a handbreadth, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text specifies six long cubits, each a cubit plus a handbreadth; Latin "ædificii" also reads "of the building" rather than "of the wall."
notes.40:9: Throughout this chapter, the Vulgate consistently translates the Hebrew architectural term for the gate's jambs or pilasters as "frons" ("front").
notes.40:17: Latin "gazophylacia" literally denotes treasury chambers or storerooms, the Vulgate's consistent rendering for the temple courtyard chambers, distinct from "thalami" ("chambers") inside the gatehouses.
notes.40:29: Verse 30, which in the Hebrew Masoretic Text adds a separate vestibule measurement, is absent from the Clementine Vulgate (as also from the Septuagint), so the numbering moves directly from 40:29 to 40:31.
notes.40:43: Latin "labia" ("rims" or "lips") reflects a Vulgate-distinct rendering of a difficult Hebrew architectural term often translated "hooks" in Masoretic-based versions.
notes.41:6: Latin latera ('sides') renders Hebrew tsela'ot ('side chambers'). Distinctively, the Vulgate reads bis triginta tria ('twice thirty-three'), interpreting the Hebrew expression for thirty chambers in three tiers with a dual multiplier.
notes.41:7: The Vulgate renders this difficult architectural verse with a circular broad passage (platea) ascending by a spiral staircase (per cochleam) into the upper room of the temple, accounting for the greater width of the upper levels.
notes.41:11: Distinctively, the Vulgate translates the Hebrew term for the open space beside the chambers (munnach) as ad orationem ('for prayer') and loci ad orationem ('of the place for prayer').
notes.41:15: Latin ethecas (also in v. 16) is Jerome's transliteration of the rare Hebrew architectural term 'attiqim, referring to projecting galleries or corridors.
notes.41:25: Where the Hebrew mentions a thick wooden canopy at the front of the vestibule, the Vulgate adds a causal connection (quam ob rem et grossiora erant ligna), explaining that the exterior timbers were thicker because of the carvings.
notes.42:1: Throughout chapters 41-42, Latin gazophylacium (literally 'treasury' or 'store-chamber') is Jerome's standard rendering for the temple chambers used to store sacred offerings and priestly vestments.
notes.42:6: Unlike the Hebrew, which describes the upper chambers as recessed and places the fifty-cubit measurement only in v. 7, the Vulgate states that they projected (eminebant) fifty cubits from the ground (a terra cubitis quinquaginta).
notes.42:13: Latin Sancta sanctorum appears twice: first spatially with in ('into the Holy of Holies') modifying the priests who draw near to the Lord, and second as the object of ponent ('the most holy things', i.e., sacred offerings). The Vulgate also joins the offerings as oblationem pro peccato et pro delicto ('the offering for sin and for trespass').
notes.42:20: Although vv. 16-19 measure five hundred reeds (calamos) along each wind, the Vulgate explicitly specifies five hundred cubits (cubitorum) for the length and width of the outer wall here.
notes.43:7: The Vulgate links 'the man who was standing beside me' (v. 6) grammatically as the subject of 'said to me' (v. 7) even though the speech is in God's first person. It also reads 'in the ruins of their kings' (Latin in ruinis regum suorum, repeated in v. 9), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has 'the corpses [or monuments] of their kings.'
notes.43:11: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which begins with a conditional clause ('And if they are ashamed...'), the Vulgate continues the jussive commands from v. 10 ('and let them be ashamed of all that they have done').
notes.43:13: The Vulgate specifies 'the truest cubit' (Latin in cubito verissimo) and 'the trench of the altar' (Latin fossa altaris), distinct from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's 'cubits' and 'base/height.'
notes.43:15: The Vulgate retains the untranslated Hebrew technical term ariel (also in v. 16), denoting the upper hearth of the altar.
notes.43:26: 'Fill its hand' translates the Latin idiom implebunt manum ejus literally, a sacrificial expression for consecrating or dedicating the altar.
notes.44:3: Following the Vulgate sentence division, 'to the prince' (Latin principi) concludes the clause of v. 2 ('it shall be closed to the prince'), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text begins a new clause in v. 3 ('As for the prince...').
notes.44:15: Here and in 43:19, the Vulgate reads 'the priests and the Levites' (Latin sacerdotes et Levitae), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has 'the Levitical priests.'
notes.44:19: The Vulgate renders the priestly rooms as the singular 'treasury of the sanctuary' (Latin in gazophylacio sanctuarii), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has 'the holy chambers.'
notes.44:23: The Vulgate renders the opposite of 'holy' as 'defiled' (Latin pollutum), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has 'common/profane.'
notes.44:28: The Vulgate states negatively 'they shall have no inheritance' (Latin Non erit autem eis haereditas), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads affirmatively ('it shall be for them an inheritance').
notes.45:1: Vulgate renders Hebrew terumah ("offering" or "allotment") as primitias ("firstfruits") here and in vv. 13 and 16, and follows the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "ten thousand" (without specifying cubits or reeds), whereas the Septuagint reads "twenty thousand."
notes.45:5: Vulgate viginti gazophylacia ("twenty treasury chambers") reflects the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("twenty chambers"), whereas the Septuagint reads "cities to dwell in."
notes.45:9: Vulgate separate confinia vestra a populo meo ("separate your borders from My people") translates the Hebrew noun as territorial boundaries rather than "evictions" or "exactions."
notes.45:11: Vulgate uses the measure cor (corus) here and in vv. 13-14 where the Hebrew Masoretic Text uses homer (both equal ten baths or ten ephahs); in v. 12, Vulgate similarly renders Hebrew gerahs with the Greek-derived weight obols (obolos).
notes.45:15: Vulgate de his quæ nutriunt Israël ("from the things that nourish Israel") translates the Hebrew expression for the "well-watered pastures of Israel" as what sustains the nation, and specifies a "ram" (arietem) rather than a generic sheep.
notes.46:6: Clementine Vulgate reads plural arietes ("rams"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text has the singular ("a ram"), which the Vulgate itself reflects in v. 7 (per arietem, "for the ram").
notes.46:11: Vulgate translates the Hebrew pilgrim festivals with Latin nundinis ("fairs" or public market-festivals), distinguishing them from the adjacent solemnitatibus ("feasts").
notes.46:14: Vulgate uses the unusual Graeco-Latin distributive idiom cata mane mane ("morning by morning") here and in v. 15, borrowing Greek kata to mirror the Hebrew repetition; vv. 13-15 also use the third-person singular ("he shall prepare") rather than the Hebrew's second-person singular (vv. 13-14) and third-person plural (v. 15).
notes.46:20: Vulgate uses coquent ("cook") for both verbs, where the Hebrew distinguishes boiling the sin and guilt offerings from baking the grain sacrifice.
notes.47:6: Vulgate renders the Hebrew question ("Have you seen, son of man?") as an emphatic affirmation, Certe vidisti, fili hominis ("Surely you have seen, son of man.").
notes.47:8: Vulgate translates Hebrew ha-gelilah ha-qadmonah ("the eastern region") as tumulos sabuli orientalis ("mounds of eastern sand"), and renders the phrase after "the sea" as a future verb, et exibunt ("and go out").
notes.47:13: Literally "a double cord/line" (duplicem funiculum), a biblical idiom for a measured allotment; Vulgate specifies "double" where the Hebrew reads simply "portions."
notes.47:16: Vulgate translates the first element of the Hebrew place names Hazer-hatticon here and Hazar-enan in v. 17 as common nouns: domus Tichon ("the house of Tichon") and atrium Enon ("the court of Enon").
notes.47:18: Vulgate Metiemini etiam plagam orientalem ("You shall also measure the eastern side") reflects a verbal reading of the Hebrew consonants normally rendered "this is the eastern side"; in v. 19, Vulgate also translates Hebrew Meriboth literally as aquas contradictionis ("the waters of contradiction").
notes.48:1: Vulgate partially translates the place name Hazar-enan as atrium Enan ("the court of Enan") and keeps the terse clause et erit ei plaga orientalis mare ("and there will be for it the eastern side, the sea"), indicating a strip extending from the eastern side to the sea as in verses 2-7.
notes.48:8: Throughout this chapter, Vulgate renders the sacred territorial allotment (Hebrew terumah) as primitiae ("firstfruits"). Likewise, Latin mare ("the sea") is kept literally where Vulgate refers to the western boundary by the Mediterranean, distinct from occidens/occidentalis ("west/western") elsewhere in the chapter.
notes.48:11: Vulgate reads sanctuarium ("the sanctuary"), taking the underlying Hebrew form as the noun "sanctuary" rather than the participle "consecrated" applied to the priests in Hebrew-based translations.
notes.48:28: Vulgate translates Meribath-kadesh literally as aquas contradictionis Cades ("the waters of contradiction of Kadesh") and renders the following term as haereditas ("an inheritance"), reading the unpointed Hebrew consonants as "inheritance" rather than "to the brook" (the Brook of Egypt).
notes.48:35: Vulgate Dominus ibidem renders the symbolic Hebrew name YHWH Shammah ("the Lord is there"), with Latin ibidem carrying the emphatic nuance "in that very place."
